one_liner: Go serialization primitives for the tagless MUS binary format; ~3x faster than protobuf-go on small structs, ~6x in unsafe mode.
what_it_does: mus-go is a set of Marshal/Unmarshal/Size/Skip serializers for Go primitives (packages varint, raw, ord, unsafe), plus pointer-mapping (pm) and typed/versioned (typed) wrappers, for the MUS format, which writes values in declaration order with no field names or tags. Structs are not supported out of the box: you implement mus.Serializer[T] per type by hand or generate it with mus-gen, a Go program that reflects over your Go types (there is no IDL). The API is caller-buffer based: call Size, allocate, Marshal into a []byte; Unmarshal returns the value, bytes consumed and an error. It is not wire- or API-compatible with Protobuf.
how_it_is_fast: The MUS format carries no field tags or type metadata, so the encoder writes values back to back and the decoder reads them positionally against a shared schema, with no tag dispatch and no reflection. Each field picks its own encoding: LEB128 varint (ZigZag for signed), fixed-width little-endian raw, or the unsafe package, which stores numbers with a pointer cast and returns strings that alias the input via unsafe.String (zero copy). A Size pass gives the exact buffer length, so a marshal costs one allocation, or none when the caller reuses a buffer.
when_to_use: Go-to-Go RPC, IPC, queue or cache payloads where both ends share the same Go types and you control deployment of both.
Hot paths with small, flat structs where per-message latency and allocations matter: in the report, mus/unsafe_reuse does 50 ns marshal / 55 ns unmarshal with 0 allocs/op in both directions.
Compact payloads: no per-field tags, and varint keeps small integers to 1 byte (49 B vs protobuf-go's 51 B on the benchmark struct).
You want validation during unmarshal (length, element, key and value validators), Skip, or partial/out-of-order decoding.
Object graphs with shared or cyclic pointers, which the pm package preserves (pointer equality survives the round trip).
when_not_to_use: You need field-level schema evolution (old readers ignoring new fields, as Protobuf does): MUS is positional; versioning is by whole-type DTM versions plus migration functions.
You need interop with the Protobuf/gRPC ecosystem or non-Go peers that already speak Protobuf; the wire format differs.
Safe mode against other fast Go codecs: in the same report plain mus (214 ns total) trails benc (184) and ties 200sc/bebop (206), and beats gogo/protobuf (281) by only ~1.3x.
You want a stable API: the project is pre-1.0 (v0.10.2), interfaces changed between minors (issue #10), and SECURITY.md only supports v0.10.x.
Decoding untrusted input with the default ord slice/map serializers: they allocate make([]T, length) from the encoded length before reading elements unless you configure a length validator.

integration.dependencies: github.com/mus-format/common-go, golang.org/x/exp (constraints); test-only: ymz-ncnk/assert, ymz-ncnk/mok; optional: mus-gen-go for code generation
integration.platforms: any Go target (pure Go; README claims 32/64-bit compatibility); unsafe-package numbers use host byte order, so they match the little-endian spec only on little-endian CPUs
integration.thread_safety: not documented. Core serializers are stateless values (safe to share by construction, per the source); pm serializers mutate shared pointer maps that Wrap resets after each call, so do not use one pm instance concurrently.

gotchas: unsafe numeric Marshal writes through *(*T)(unsafe.Pointer(&bs[0])) and bounds-checks only bs[0]: a too-short buffer gives an out-of-bounds write, not the panic the safe packages raise, and bytes come out in host order.

unsafe.String results alias the input buffer; mutating or reusing that buffer changes the decoded strings (the README warns about this). With buffer reuse, the next Marshal overwrites the previously returned slice.
In the current main branch, unsafe ByteSlice.Unmarshal still calls make([]byte, length) before returning the aliasing slice, so it is not zero-allocation.
The benchmark measured mus-go v0.3.0 (function-style API such as ord.MarshalString); v0.10.x uses mus.Serializer[T] values, so the harness code does not compile against current releases as-is.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick mus-go over benc, gencode and 200sc/bebop (Go) when you can accept unsafe strings and buffer reuse: mus/unsafe_reuse is the fastest non-baseline row in the shared report (105 ns total, 0 allocs) ahead of benc/usafe (121 ns) and gencode/unsafe_reuse (152 ns). In safe mode it has no speed edge over benc or bebop; pick it then for per-field varint/raw choice, validators, Skip, pointer mapping and typed versioning.
verified_claims_summary: alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks report (data.js, regenerated 2025-07-04; no CPU listed; harness go.mod says Go 1.22.4) on a SmallStruct of two strings, a time, an int, a bool and a float64: hand-written mus-go v0.3.0 marshals/unmarshals in 92/122 ns/op against protobuf-go v1.34.2's 287/356 ns/op (~3.1x/2.9x), and the unsafe_reuse variant in 50/55 ns/op (~5.7x/6.5x) with 0 allocs. The author's own suite (Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Go 1.23.5, mus-go v0.6.2) shows a similar gap: 102.9 ns round trip vs 531.7 ns for protobuf and 192.5 ns for vtprotobuf.
status_note: Actively maintained (v0.10.2 released 2026-05-06, last main commit 2026-05-07), MIT-licensed pure Go with CI fuzzing and CodeQL, but pre-1.0 with API changes between minor versions.
